_: The full candidate set from the 28 Jul 2026 naming run. Generated by 13 subagents, one naming direction each; 213 raised, 197 unique. Availability was RDAP-checked at the time and is NOT rechecked here — re-verify before acting on any of it. Narrative and current standing: ../../naming-domains.md

candidates.m: The room where you keep what you'll need later. In ornithology 'larder-hoarding' is the real term for a bird stashing everything in one place, and the shrike's spike of stored prey is literally called its larder.
candidates.p: Everything you're keeping, in one place, ready when you come back for it.
candidates.c: none - larder.com is a blank 200, no product
candidates.r: low - plain English word, no live brand on it, no bird required to get the joke
candidates.mine: My #1. Plain English, warm, and 'larder-hoarding' is the real biological term for caching everything in one place — so it sits directly beside the 'hoard' you already like, without reusing the word.

candidates.m: A garner is a granary — the building grain is stored in. It is also the verb 'to garner': to gather and store up. Same word, both halves.
candidates.p: Everything you've gathered, kept somewhere it won't rot.
candidates.c: garner.com redirects to telepathy.com, a premium-domain brokerage — parked, no product
candidates.r: low — real English word, one meaning, no live product on it
candidates.mine: Noun and verb in a single short word: a garner IS a granary, and to garner is to gather and store. Rare to get both.

candidates.m: Old Norse verb 'muna' = to remember. It is the exact root Munin's name is built from (munr = mind/memory).
candidates.p: The verb behind the raven. Same world, same art, same everything - you just say the thing instead of naming the bird.
candidates.c: muna.com is Demitri Muna's personal academic page (astronomer). No product.
candidates.r: low - real word, no product on the .com, keeps the whole Munin identity intact
candidates.mine: The cleanest rename that isn't a rebrand — every raven drawing, the perch logo, the ink teal and the hoard all survive untouched, because this is literally the verb the name Munin is built from.

candidates.m: to press a mark into a surface — and, in the same breath, to fix something in someone's memory ('impress it on your mind'). Same verb, both senses, since Latin imprimere.
candidates.p: Press it in until it stays. That's the whole thing.
candidates.c: impress.com is a personal redirect to a LinkedIn profile (Joshua Schoen, Helix House) — not a product
candidates.r: low — no product on the .com; only mild overlap with the everyday 'impress people' sense
candidates.mine: Means a mark pressed into a surface AND a memory, with 'one pull of the press' = one repetition underneath. Watch that it also means showing off.

candidates.m: A hornbook was the paddle-shaped leaf of alphabet, numbers and the Lord's Prayer, protected under a sheet of transparent horn, that English children learned to read from for three centuries — the first flashcard
candidates.p: The oldest flashcard in English, five hundred years on.
candidates.c: hornbook.com is a registrar parking lander — no product
candidates.r: low — obscure enough that you have to explain it once, but it explains beautifully and suits the hand-drawn identity
candidates.mine: Found independently by three lanes. A hornbook is the physical ancestor of the flashcard — an alphabet paddle under a sheet of horn.

candidates.m: A bearing is the direction to a landmark; two crossed bearings give you your position. 'Get your bearings' is the everyday form.
candidates.p: Open it and you know where you stand. That's the whole product.
candidates.c: bearings.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — plain English word, no live .com, reads as orientation not edtech

candidates.m: Change-ringers: the English bell-ringing bands who memorise hundreds of 'methods' by heart, no sheet music, and ring them in a tower on a rota.
candidates.p: 'I'm in the ringers club' is the best sentence on this list. Ringers are the purest amateur memory club Britain ever produced — a band of people who keep a hard thing in their heads by turning up.
candidates.c: none/dead
candidates.r: low - 'ringer' also means an impostor in sport, but the plural reads as the bell sense
candidates.mine: Best sentence on the list and the best story. Only caveat: 'a ringer' also means an impostor or a substitute.

candidates.m: The stone you draw a blade across, pass after pass, to bring back the edge. 'Whet' is Old English for sharpen; the stone is the oldest tool of deliberate repetition there is.
candidates.p: The edge doesn't come from one pass. It comes from going back to the stone.
candidates.c: whetstone.com resolves but serves a 311-byte blank page — parked, no product.
candidates.r: med — the exact .com is empty, but Whetstone Education (instructional coaching) and Whetstone Magazine both exist on longer domains

candidates.m: The western scrub jay is the bird in the famous memory experiments — it caches thousands of items and remembers what it hid, where, and how long ago. It is a corvid, so it is family to the raven, without being the raven.
candidates.p: The bird that remembers where it put every single thing.
candidates.c: scrubjay.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low-med — two words joined; still one clear bird
candidates.mine: The scrub jay is the bird in the landmark episodic-memory experiments — a corvid that isn't a used-up corvid word.

candidates.m: Military: muster is the roll call where every name is checked present. 'To muster' is also to summon something up on demand — and 'passing muster' is being found good enough on inspection
candidates.p: Daily muster. Everything you know, called out and present.
candidates.c: muster.com is dead — no site
candidates.r: low-med — 'muster' also has an unrelated German sense (pattern/sample) for European ears
candidates.mine: Came back from three separate lanes independently.

candidates.m: Icelandic pet-name for a raven — the affectionate one, not the formal 'hrafn'. Star of the folk song 'Krummi svaf i klettagja'.
candidates.p: Munin's own language has a nickname for the bird. This is it — same raven, off duty.
candidates.c: none — krummi.com does not resolve
candidates.r: low — Krummi Bjorgvinsson is a mid-tier Icelandic rock singer; no product, no bad meaning found in any language checked

candidates.m: Theatre: the understudy learns every line, cue and move for a part they may never actually play — the purest case of knowing something cold before you need it
candidates.p: Know it cold long before anyone asks you to perform it.
candidates.c: understudy.com is a personal Substack newsletter — no product
candidates.r: low — four syllables is the only cost; the metaphor lands with no explanation

candidates.m: Falconry: a brancher is a young bird that has left the nest and is hopping branch to branch, not yet properly flying. The stage where you're doing it but not well yet.
candidates.p: You're out of the nest and not flying yet. That's the whole point of this thing.
candidates.c: none - brancher.com is a blank 200
candidates.r: low - reads as English, spells itself, no brand on it

candidates.m: Scots for a raven or crow - from the ballad 'The Twa Corbies', two crows sitting on a wall talking about what they remember. The folk word, not the Latin one.
candidates.p: The raven, in the old vernacular. Two of them on a wall, going over it again.
candidates.c: none - corbie.com is a blank parked page
candidates.r: low - keeps the raven identity without using a rejected raven word

candidates.m: Two things at once: the coverts are the feathers that cover the base of a bird's flight feathers, and a covert is a hiding place. What's cached is covered until you go and get it.
candidates.p: It's covered over until you need it. Then you know exactly where it was.
candidates.c: none - covert.com 301s to a blank https page
candidates.r: low-med - spells itself, but people split on COH-vert vs cuh-VERT

candidates.m: A store for grain. The acorn woodpecker drills a 'granary tree' with thousands of holes, one acorn per hole, and comes back to them all winter - the closest thing in nature to a card deck.
candidates.p: Drill one hole per fact, come back all winter, nothing rots.
candidates.c: none - granary.com 301s to a blank page, dead
candidates.r: low - warm and spellable; only baggage is granary bread

candidates.m: Falconry: mantling is when a bird hunches and spreads its wings over its food so nothing can take it. The bird guarding its hoard.
candidates.p: Wings over the thing you worked for. Nobody takes it off you.
candidates.c: none - mantling.com is a blank 200. (Note: plain mantle.com belongs to Synopsys and Mantle is an Ethereum L2, which is exactly why this is the 'mantling' spelling.)
candidates.r: low - clean domain; slightly longer to type than the one-word options

candidates.m: The Edda - the two books that caught Norse oral memory on parchment before it was lost, and the source of everything we know about Munin.
candidates.p: The book that saved the memory. Yours is the same job, one card at a time.
candidates.c: edda.com does not resolve. Dead.
candidates.r: low - four letters, no collision, sits inside the existing world

candidates.m: Old Norse 'hodd' = hoard, treasure. The actual word behind the English 'hoard' you already use for the badges.
candidates.p: You already call the badges the hoard. This is the word they were called first.
candidates.c: hodd.com does not resolve. Dead.
candidates.r: med - the double d is the one spelling wobble (hod vs hodd)

candidates.m: Old Norse 'stef' = the refrain a skald threads back through a drapa at fixed intervals. Spaced repetition, named in 10th-century poetics.
candidates.p: The line the poem keeps coming back to, on a schedule. That's the whole product in four letters.
candidates.c: stef.com is STEF, a French cold-chain food logistics group. Big company, unrelated sector, not an app.
candidates.r: med - the .com is a real corporate, and 'Stef' also reads as a first name

candidates.m: A flashbulb memory is the vivid, permanent kind you get from a shock — Brown and Kulik, 1977. Also: flash cards.
candidates.p: Cards that stick like the memories you never had to study for.
candidates.c: flashbulb.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — the only name here that means the mechanism AND the format at the same time

candidates.m: Relearning savings — Ebbinghaus's own measure: forgotten material comes back faster the second time. The forgetting was never total.
candidates.p: Forgot it? Fine. Getting it back is cheap. That's the whole method.
candidates.c: relearn.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — reads as the honest version of what an SRS actually does all day

candidates.m: The memory trace is the physical record a memory leaves behind; to retrace is to walk the same path a second time.
candidates.p: You already learned it once. This walks you back over it before it goes.
candidates.c: retrace.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — plain English verb, no live product on the .com, and the double meaning is exact rather than cute

candidates.m: Retrieval is the act of pulling a memory out — and pulling it out is what strengthens it, not putting it in.
candidates.p: Not re-reading. Pulling it out of your head cold, which is the part that works.
candidates.c: retrieve.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — a verb people already use, and the correct verb for this app

candidates.m: Theatre: your cue line is the line immediately before yours, the trigger. Actors rehearse cue-and-line pairs — which is literally the two sides of a flashcard
candidates.p: Cue on one side, line on the other. Actors invented the flashcard and called it this.
candidates.c: cueline.com is dead — no site
candidates.r: low-med — 'cue' can be heard as 'queue' or 'Q' by non-theatre people

candidates.m: In Scots and northern English 'to ken' is to know — 'd'ye ken?'. A kenning is also the Norse poetic compound where a raven is a 'corpse-swan': the same literature Munin comes out of
candidates.p: Ken it, don't just read it. Scots for knowing, Norse for the poetry.
candidates.c: kenning.com is a registrar parking lander — no product
candidates.r: low — the double meaning is a feature; only risk is people hearing it as a surname

candidates.m: Dead reckoning: knowing where you are purely from what you logged — course, speed, time — with nothing outside to check against. It's the core skill of the RYA courses already shipped
candidates.p: Dead reckoning for your head. You know where you are because you kept the log.
candidates.c: reckoning.com is a for-sale parking page — no product
candidates.r: med — 'day of reckoning' drags a bit of doom in with it

candidates.m: Drumming: the forty rudiments are the fixed sticking patterns every drummer drills for years until they run without conscious thought — the trade's own word for over-learning
candidates.p: Drill the rudiments. Everything you can actually do sits on top of them.
candidates.c: rudiments.com is a registrar parking lander — no product
candidates.r: low-med — outside drumming it can read as 'basics only', which undersells

candidates.m: Latin gerundive of repetere: 'the things that must be repeated'. The unclaimed sibling of agenda and memoranda.
candidates.p: The things that must be repeated. That's not a tagline, that's the product.
candidates.c: repetenda.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: med — unfamiliar word, needs one line of explanation, but reads correctly on sight

candidates.m: From Latin revisere, 'to go back and look at a thing again' — re- (again) + visere (to go see). The plainest classical statement of spaced repetition.
candidates.p: You don't relearn it. You revisit it, on the day it needs revisiting.
candidates.c: revisit.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — everyday word, one possible spelling, and the nearest living cousin to the 'revise' he already likes

candidates.m: To bring a metal surface to a hard bright finish by rubbing it over and over with a smooth tool. Nothing is added — the shine is purely the repetition.
candidates.p: Nothing new goes on. You just keep going over it until it shines.
candidates.c: burnish.com resolves to an empty page — parked.
candidates.r: low — clean word, no product owns it, spells itself

candidates.m: The stone a cave builds from dripping water — stalactites and flowstone. Each drop leaves almost nothing; the column is thousands of years of almost nothing.
candidates.p: One drop leaves nothing behind. Enough drops build stone.
candidates.c: dripstone.com serves a 403 error page — no product, no content.
candidates.r: low — spells itself, no brand on it, and it's the cleanest picture of compounding I found

candidates.m: The sound and count of steps. In retail it means how many people came through; in a wood it's what wears the path into the ground.
candidates.p: One step is nothing. Enough footfall and there's a path.
candidates.c: footfall.com is dead — no response.
candidates.r: low — spells itself, no live product, and the counting sense fits a streak app

candidates.m: A ditty box is the small personal chest a sailor keeps letters, needles and trinkets in. A ditty is also a short tune you can't stop remembering — both senses land on the same product.
candidates.p: Small box, small things worth keeping, opened often.
candidates.c: dittybox.com returns an empty page — parked
candidates.r: low — obscure but instantly likeable once explained

candidates.m: The archaeological term for the exact place an object came out of the ground. A hoard without its findspot loses most of its meaning — where you found it is part of what it is.
candidates.p: Every card remembers where you found it.
candidates.c: findspot.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low-med — jargon, but self-explaining once seen

candidates.m: A midden is a refuse heap — and the single richest thing on an archaeological dig. Packrat middens in the American west preserve 50,000-year records of what grew there.
candidates.p: The pile you keep adding to turns into the record of what you knew.
candidates.c: midden.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: med — the literal sense is 'rubbish heap'; charming if you explain it, odd if you don't

candidates.m: The archetypal hoarding animal. It caches everything it finds, and palaeoclimatologists read those caches as archives.
candidates.p: Keep everything. It turns out that's the good strategy.
candidates.c: packrat.com sits behind Incapsula with no content — believed to be the 1-800-PACK-RAT moving/storage company
candidates.r: med — a US storage brand shares the word, though a different market

candidates.m: A sailor's sea chest: the one box you own, holding your tools, papers and keepsakes for the whole voyage. Sits directly on top of the RYA courses.
candidates.p: One box, everything you need to know aboard, in the order you need it.
candidates.c: seachest.com returns an empty page — parked
candidates.r: low — nautical, warm, no live product

candidates.m: The universal amateur archive — the shoebox under the bed with the photos, ticket stubs and letters in it. Everybody has one.
candidates.p: The shoebox under the bed, except it hands things back to you.
candidates.c: shoebox.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — plain, warm, zero explanation needed

candidates.m: The archaeologist's hand tool. Hoards come out of the ground a trowel-scrape at a time, never a shovel at a time.
candidates.p: Twenty minutes a day with a small tool. That's how anything big gets uncovered.
candidates.c: trowel.com shows 'Trowel.com -> Offline' — dead
candidates.r: low — concrete object, no edtech smell, unusual

candidates.m: The sung evening office — the service you come back to at the same hour every single day.
candidates.p: 'I'm in the evensong club' sounds like belonging to something warm and old. It's the daily-return ritual with a tune, which is exactly the habit the app is selling.
candidates.c: evensong.com is one man's personal homepage (Robert Reese Hershey), not a product
candidates.r: low - faintly churchy, but reads as English and gentle rather than devout

candidates.m: A litany is a recitation of call and response, repeated line by line by a whole congregation; colloquially, a long list gone through in order.
candidates.p: 'I'm in the litany club' — call and response, in order, again. That is the interaction model of a flashcard described in one four-hundred-year-old word.
candidates.c: litany.com is a novelist's personal homepage (John B. Olson), not a product
candidates.r: low-med - 'a litany of complaints' gives it a faintly weary tone

candidates.m: The ship's log — filled in every watch, by whoever is on duty, without exception.
candidates.p: 'I'm in the logbook club' is a club defined by a discipline you keep, which is the whole product. Munin already prints a ship's log; this makes it the name.
candidates.c: none/dead
candidates.r: low - plain word, slightly utilitarian

candidates.m: The first office of the day, sung before dawn — the morning half of the same monastic clock as evensong.
candidates.p: 'I'm in the matins club' is what you say if you do your cards before anyone else is awake. It gives the morning session a name and a slight badge of honour.
candidates.c: matins.com is a registrar parking page ('a successful business needs a successful address')
candidates.r: low - some will hear 'matinees'; short enough to correct once

candidates.m: Coined compound: 'lore' = the body of stuff you're supposed to know, 'keep' = the stone tower where a thing is kept safe. Reads on sight, has never been a word.
candidates.p: Everything you're meant to know, kept somewhere it can't leak out.
candidates.c: none — lorekeep.com does not respond at all (dead)
candidates.r: low — no live .com, nothing to confuse it with; 'Lorekeeper' exists as a niche open-source fansite tool, different word

candidates.m: Remember and bird welded at the shared 'b': re-mem-bird. The whole product in one word — the memory bird.
candidates.p: The bird remembers so you don't have to guess whether you do.
candidates.c: none — remembird.com is dead; a discontinued birdwatching voice-recorder once used the name
candidates.r: low — dead .com, defunct hardware namesake in an unrelated category

candidates.m: Portuguese 'remembers'. 'Lembra?' is how a Brazilian asks you 'remember?'.
candidates.p: The way a Brazilian asks 'remember?' — which is the only question the app ever asks.
candidates.c: none — lembra.com does not resolve
candidates.r: low-med — it is a bare verb form, so it reads slightly unfinished to a Portuguese speaker

candidates.m: Spanish for a revision — literally a re-pass, going over the material one more time.
candidates.p: 'Revise' in Spanish, and it sounds like what it does: another pass.
candidates.c: repaso.com resolves but serves no title — parked, no product
candidates.r: low — it is the plain common noun, used by Spanish-language tutoring sites, so descriptive rather than distinctive

candidates.m: Turkish for 'again' — and for 'a repetition'. The one word that is both.
candidates.p: Again. That's what the app asks you every morning, so that's the name.
candidates.c: tekrar.com is a HugeDomains for-sale parking page
candidates.r: low — no notable holder, no unfortunate reading found; scans cleanly in English

candidates.m: The birds all singing at first light. Happens every morning without anyone organising it.
candidates.p: First light, everything you owe, all at once. Then quiet for the rest of the day.
candidates.c: dawnchorus.com resolves but serves an empty page — no product
candidates.r: low — birds tie straight to the raven identity; two words is the only cost

candidates.m: The 4-8am watch at sea. The one you're dreading until you're on deck for the sunrise.
candidates.p: Take the morning watch. Cards before coffee, done before the day starts.
candidates.c: morningwatch.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — a bit long, and 'watch' can read as wearable/video

candidates.m: The sun sight a navigator takes at local noon, every single day, to fix the ship's position.
candidates.p: Same time every day, one measurement, and you know where you are.
candidates.c: noonsight.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — lands perfectly with the Day Skipper crowd, opaque to everyone else

candidates.m: The fixed daily portion issued to each person aboard. Not more, not less, and it arrives every day.
candidates.p: Today's ration of cards. Small enough to finish, and there's another tomorrow.
candidates.c: rations.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — 'rationing' can read as scarcity rather than pacing

candidates.m: Three times. Lewis Carroll's Bellman: 'What I tell you three times is true.'
candidates.p: Nothing sticks the first time. Third pass and it's yours.
candidates.c: thrice.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — a band called Thrice exists, but no domain and no category overlap

candidates.m: The book of tides every sailor checks before leaving. Fixed, predictable, consulted daily.
candidates.p: The schedule is already worked out. You just read off what's happening today.
candidates.c: tidetable.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — RYA-native; slight double-t stumble when typed fast

candidates.m: Evening prayer in the Divine Office — the fixed hour you come back to at dusk.
candidates.p: Your evening hour. The cards are already waiting, you just show up.
candidates.c: vespers.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — reads monastic rather than churchy, and the .com is empty

candidates.m: Chartwork is the RYA's own word for the plotting exercises you grind through for Day Skipper — the drill part of the syllabus.
candidates.p: The drill, named the way your Day Skipper course names it.
candidates.c: chartwork.com resolves but serves an empty page — parked
candidates.r: low — no live product; niche-sounding to a non-sailor but instantly right to anyone who's sat the exam

candidates.m: The verb form of dead reckoning — to work your position forward from the last thing you knew for certain.
candidates.p: Work forward from the last thing you knew for certain. Every session moves the mark.
candidates.c: deadreckon.com does not resolve — dead
candidates.r: low — clean; 'dead' is the only word that might read heavy

candidates.m: A running fix: you take a bearing, carry it forward over the hours you've run, then cross it with a fresh one. An old observation kept alive and combined with a new one.
candidates.p: Spaced repetition already had a name at sea. Old sighting plus new sighting equals knowing exactly where you are.
candidates.c: runningfix.com is a HugeDomains for-sale page — parked
candidates.r: low — parked .com, zero product collision; slightly jargon on first read
candidates.mine: A running fix is an old bearing carried forward and crossed with a new one. Navigators described spaced repetition before psychologists did.

candidates.m: the stub of a ticket or cheque — the half you tear off and keep as your own record of what happened.
candidates.p: The half you keep. Your record of what you've actually learned.
candidates.c: counterfoil.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — dead .com, no collision anywhere; eleven letters is the only cost

candidates.m: the Leitner box — the physical card box with dated compartments that Sebastian Leitner invented in 1972. It is the direct ancestor of every spaced-repetition app, including this one.
candidates.p: The Leitner box, without the box. Cards move back when you miss them.

candidates.r: med — the concept fit is unbeatable, but it's a German surname and a real company owns the .com

candidates.m: the library code that says exactly where a book lives on the shelf — and, read plainly, a mark made by pressing. Both halves of the brief in one word.
candidates.p: A mark pressed in, and a place to find it again. That's memory.
candidates.c: pressmark.com is a parked GoDaddy lander
candidates.r: low — parked .com, no product anywhere in the space

candidates.m: the front side of a leaf of paper (its back is the verso). A flashcard is exactly a recto and a verso — the question and the answer, one sheet.

candidates.c: recto.com is a 'Coming Soon' placeholder — parked
candidates.r: low — parked .com; the word is bookish, so some people meet it for the first time here

candidates.m: a fresh impression pulled from the original plate years after the first run. The plate is still there; you just print from it again.
candidates.p: The plate doesn't wear out. Pull another impression when it's due.
candidates.c: restrike.com is dead — no response
candidates.r: low — dead .com; 'strike' is slightly forceful for a gentle product

candidates.m: Welsh, roughly 'blessed raven' - Branwen of the Mabinogi, sister of Bran the Blessed whose buried head is said to guard Britain. It's also the name of one of the actual ravens at the Tower of London right now.
candidates.p: Named for a raven that's still on the payroll at the Tower.
candidates.c: none reachable - branwen.com sits behind a Cloudflare challenge, no product visible
candidates.r: med - gorgeous, but it reads as a woman's name before it reads as a product

candidates.m: Falconry: the cadge is the padded wooden frame a falconer carries several hooded hawks on out to the field. A rack you carry your birds on.
candidates.p: The frame you carry the whole lot on. One rack, all your birds.
candidates.c: cadge.com is a domain-broker sales page, no product
candidates.r: med - 'cadge' also means to scrounge, and that meaning is more common in the UK

candidates.m: Falconry: the long light line that keeps a hawk tethered while it's being trained to come back - you fly it on the creance until it's reliable, then you let it go free.
candidates.p: On the line until it comes back every time. Then off the line.

candidates.r: med - the metaphor is exact but nobody outside falconry knows the word

candidates.m: The bright bib of colour on a bird's throat - the field-guide word for the patch you use to tell one species from another. Originally a piece of throat armour.
candidates.p: The marking that tells you what you're looking at.
candidates.c: none - gorget.com returns 410 gone
candidates.r: med - lovely to look at, but you'd spell it aloud every time

candidates.m: A raven's hackles are the shaggy lance-shaped throat feathers it flares when it calls - the single most raven-specific bit of anatomy there is.
candidates.p: Throat feathers up, saying it out loud until it sticks.
candidates.c: none - hackle.com is dead (436); hackles.com is a 'coming soon' placeholder
candidates.r: med - 'raise your hackles' pulls toward irritation, not memory
